> A handheld thermal camera built around an MLX90640 32x24 IR sensor and an ESP32-S3. It streams the thermal image to a 2.0" IPS display with interpolation and a color palette, and runs off a single-cell LiPo with USB-C charging. I'm designing the custom 2-layer PCB myself, with the sensor kept away from heat sources like the regulator and charger, and a 3D-printed enclosure around it.

## Design

### 2026-10-07 – October 6: Finished the schematic for my handheld thermal camera

**9h**

October 6: Finished the schematic for my handheld thermal camera

I spent 9 hours on the full schematic in EasyEDA Pro before drawing any traces. I haven't ordered or built the PCB yet, so I wanted every connection checked on paper first.

The camera uses an MLX90640 thermal sensor (32×24 pixels) and an ESP32-S3. A 2.0" screen shows the image, and a single LiPo battery powers everything, charged over USB-C.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/a15bf9552ab2d0f257fbd07564eeb48342dae4017ae386a922bdba33771a6889.png)

I split the circuit into blocks:

USB-C input. Two 5.1 kΩ resistors on the CC pins tell chargers to supply 5 V. A USBLC6-2SC6 protects the data lines, which go straight to the ESP32's built-in USB pins (IO19/IO20).

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/94d370d29630de52e4dbb25fce7799225b1e5d36d017b5d5f30f7754e28dca93.png)

Charging. A TP4056 charges the battery. A 2 kΩ resistor on its PROG pin sets about 0.6 A. Two red LEDs show charging and full, each through 1 kΩ from the 5 V line.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/d7d27e97fcc62e29ec2c62474490251bcad4ad0e2d4a0decc634521e6e04d644.png)

Battery protection. A DW01A and an FS8205A guard against over-discharge, over-charge and short circuits. I followed the standard wiring: 100 Ω and 100 nF on the supply, and 2 kΩ on the sense pin.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/bacb8ab1376ad6555a67919ea0cf8f7c6aa061f24e68ecaa4bc8597c1798045d.png)

Power. A slide switch connects the battery to the system. An AP2112K steps that down to 3.3 V with 10 µF capacitors on both sides.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/38bc08ebf0f5f946183b08d9748913c4e53e8c5f53a61ae582de8464fa56abb8.png)

Sensor. The MLX90640 uses I2C on IO1/IO2 with 4.7 kΩ pull-ups and a 100 nF capacitor close by.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/bb2614ddc9785a7b3790586f5c1aab24ba9d98d889a00e583d50c23fedecffcf.png)

Screen. An 8-pin header carries SPI to the LCD: SCK on IO12, MOSI on IO11, CS on IO10, DC on IO9, RST on IO8 and backlight on IO13. I used the ESP32-S3's default SPI pins.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/4f9224707824272e3867c852909ac59d666a1cd19cc8c1d278f2140e359dc5b7.png)

Controls. Reset, boot and trigger buttons, plus a battery-voltage divider on IO4. I picked IO4 because it's safe to read while Wi-Fi is running.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/17ff725becce24223c9d261f7a02eaa83b2177cab8ba7aa392a4afa86ae90011.png)

All of these connect to the ESP32-S3 module.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/b1aaf05b5e680ac600e0771521d756e5ce9a9b985b1d72cf03b6ce1ee68be10b.png)

While checking my work I found some challenges I faced-

1. Getting the battery circuit right. The charger and the protection chips (DW01A and FS8205A) have to be wired together in a specific way, and the datasheet pin names didn't map obviously to my schematic. I traced the current path from the battery through the protection MOSFETs to ground to check it.

2. Checking the thermal sensor's pins. The MLX90640 comes in a small 4-pin metal can. When I compared my schematic symbol to the datasheet, the pin order didn't match: the datasheet lists SDA, VDD, GND, SCL, but my symbol had them in a different order. If I had routed the board as it was, the data line would have landed on the power pin.

3. Running from USB. My schematic charges the battery from USB, but the rest of the circuit only runs from the battery. That means the camera can't be powered or flashed from USB alone. I can't just connect USB power to the system, because it would push 5 V into the battery.

4. Matching the screen's pins. Different 2" LCD modules use different pin orders. My header follows one specific order (GND, 3V3, SCK, MOSI, RST, DC, CS, BL), so I have to buy a module with that order.

5. Choosing ESP32 pins. I wanted pins that work with Wi-Fi on, so I put the battery sense on IO4, which is safe to read while Wi-Fi runs. I also used the ESP32-S3's default SPI pins for the screen, and its built-in USB pins for the USB data lines.

Next I'll finish the layout, run the design-rule check.
Time spent this session: 9 hours

### 2026-10-08 – October 7: Placed and routed the PCB for my handheld thermal camera

**13h**

October 7: Placed and routed the PCB for my handheld thermal camera

I spent 13 hours turning my schematic into a real PCB layout in EasyEDA Pro. The board is about 92 × 116 mm, and every part from the schematic is now placed and connected.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/702325fdaf3d3ccb4b31970609de3638bb52a565109e28596a7b8c08973a6c3c.png)

Hours 1-2: Planning the layout and the USB-C end
I started by deciding where the big parts go. The USB-C connector sits on the bottom edge so the cable plugs in from outside, and it hangs slightly past the board edge. I put the ESD chip (D1) right next to the connector, with the two CC resistors (R1 and R2) beside it. The TP4056 charger (U3) is next to those, so the 5 V traces stay short.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/17b6997df9e54480f9562a50ea8745bc0c7aed89cc10bbe66b34873c94bb2756.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/2410fd10ee9c5d949ad7e92012991d62f77fe568af98b4f127329a0952dd724b.png)

Hours 3-4: Battery, protection and power switch
I grouped the battery parts together on the lower left. The battery connector (U5) has the DW01A (U4) and the FS8205 (Q1) next to it, with their small resistors and capacitor close by so the protection traces are short. The slide switch (SW1) sits nearby, and the two LEDs sit beside the charger resistors (R4 and R5). I also added my name and the project title on the silkscreen.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/cb34e8998198d000e2b5caa26b4c67340a75c2228f9ab9148c0a829a23e9b91d.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/f5d27703a0942167c593de9de57e487343cab1dfae58cabfdd5172047ce144c1.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/5428227b5e9342e56466b01094beb9d958b76ce170160144a8ff817eadc87c39.png)

Hours 5-7: ESP32 and the thermal sensor
The ESP32-S3 module is in the top right with its antenna toward the board's top edge. I placed its small capacitors and the enable resistor (C6, C8, C9, R8) right beside its pins. The MLX90640 is in the top left and mounts on the bottom of the board, with its metal can facing out the back and its pins coming through to the top. I put the I2C pull-up resistors (R11, R12) and the 100 nF capacitor (C10) on the path between the sensor and the ESP32 and routed the data lines through them.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/6908fa95951e79f6da2d128f08ef5084f431c20da9df7fb7ba6f034f738e4eee.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/7fe6d4812e35013a20538e336b75eb08088b452251c6c738a829375db9c39a29.png)

Hours 8-9: Buttons and the screen header
The three buttons (reset, boot and trigger) line up along the right edge, so a thumb can reach them. The 8-pin LCD header is in the middle of the board, and the screen will sit on top of it. I routed the SPI lines from the ESP32 down to the header.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/2b84dd8e43359d1f08ac7550def4deb2c26350dd08f300e9ad39a9210b765c2b.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/b3582e60a645fe8a12eb8bbadccba0851a95148e353d50c0e67a46c6323eec5d.png)

Hours 10-11: Routing and copper pour
I routed the remaining signals, widened the power traces, and filled the empty space with copper pour so the board has a solid ground. The bottom layer is mostly pour, with only a few traces. I checked the board in 3D from both sides to make sure the sensor can sticks out the back and nothing collides.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/328ae4eb469227a7bda33fb05f42495d9f78bd2f92871452dfad90953d65b4de.png)

Hour 12: Final checks
I went over the layout against the schematic and looked for problems.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/8a5b8179db332693fd255a862ddbb7fb1fb9a8d58fee93b1762e4b234349d7fc.png)

Hour 13: Full Display + PCB
Added a CAD of the screen to finish the look of the PCB

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/3d2cb9ddcfed1f76a8033a3acbf6ac5e098c3db9740c174ec9ed35a65ed423c2.png)

Next steps:
- Add a keepout under the ESP32 antenna. Right now there's copper pour under it, and the antenna needs it clear.
- Re-check the MLX90640 pin order between the schematic and the footprint.
- Add mounting holes and trim the board size.
- Add a path to power the circuit from USB.
- Run the design-rule check
-make a CAD model for the casing

Time spent this session: 13 hours

### 2026-10-09 – Hour 1: Measured the board. I put the PCB, the LCD and the battery into one assembly and wrapped them in a clear box. This showed the space the casing has to cover: about 93 × 117 mm, with 8 mm below

**13h**

Hour 1: Measured the board. I put the PCB, the LCD and the battery into one assembly and wrapped them in a clear box. This showed the space the casing has to cover: about 93 × 117 mm, with 8 mm below the board and 11 mm above it.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/ef7e94fc7d4d3be7659ec5f92330b64dccb1d71dde529ee2975a7e90fb32be49.png)

Hour 2: Blank back shell. I made the back tray with rounded corners, 2.4 mm walls and a stepped chamfer on the bottom edge. I left it plain so I could check the walls.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/f685053720d5fc161e75133ea83f13b4738f96cbabba21b9b3abb07a6cedbdf5.png)

Hour 3: Posts, sensor window and USB-C. I added four corner screw posts, a round window for the thermal sensor, and a rectangular cutout for the USB-C port.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/50cb9d2d7a75ca2085ca81c50f17a57409ac1549302903d2647fc4aa7f792001.png)

Hour 4: Sensor horn. The sensor sees about 110° × 75°, so a plain hole would block its view. I built a flared funnel around the window, added 8 triangular fins to strengthen it, and put an orange trim ring on the tip.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/0d52e3c189fca4aa72b2ac10dac5ec34fe8b549869bac0db0facb8efc79b9ec3.png)

Hour 5: Vents and armor bars. I cut a hex vent field through the back floor, added chevron armor bars on the back face and cut grip grooves down both sides.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/425b4093f44df3ce8c01bd01c9203500fe70322174a2500f74ef9783c163fc60.png)

Hour 6: Eye, tripod boss and rail. I added a lanyard eye on the right side and a slotted accessory rail on the top edge. I also added a hexagonal boss for a 1/4"-20 tripod nut. The nut pocket stops short of the floor so a screw can’t reach the battery.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/da33c5444495b29076ac2b1546c419ffa78c11c6d31ace3cb37e99c2766b954f.png)

Hour 7: Blank front bezel. I made the matching front plate with an LCD window, three button holes, a slider slot and a USB-C cutout.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/bc1c230076929ae981a91889957da0e50ff68257f91de4896e40252ae57e9c9c.png)

Hour 8: LCD visor. I added a wedge-shaped sun-visor around the LCD window, tall on the top edge and sloping down toward the bottom.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/f0bf75ade5080ea49a10a33368a86487d851c9c1a9f2d4fa5bb0bc409e6a0382.png)

Hour 9: Guard pill and grooves. I added a raised guard pill around the three buttons and cut diagonal vent grooves above the ESP32. I also cut grip grooves on the side walls of the bezel.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/19c159126a825ef4d831e08aa8742eadd768e48d0183bdb535e35b89bd32da77.png)

Hour 10: Caps and slider. I made three tall orange button caps and a slider knob with a fin on top. Each cap has a wide inner flange so it can’t pull out through its hole. The knob drops in from above.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/5056a12a1de64acdffe989267c6b865adc01801bd277f1d057e2d29e85a867a2.png)

Hour 11: Corner bumpers. I added four orange corner bumpers meant to be printed in TPU. They wrap the corners and leave the lanyard eye free. At the bottom-right I had to trim the bumper so it didn’t collide with the eye.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/2cee89a01ce896bb68f0f63e7b22afe7e177f109138baa4eea1a9e05b1c62829.png)

Hour 12: Exploded view. I pulled the model apart to check the order: back shell, board with LCD and battery, front bezel, then the caps. It confirmed that the parts stack and the caps and knob can be inserted.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/ead1b6a8b4ffe59db76989924ae807d32c0607fe8c793b058a17e27be9d27470.png)

Hour 13: Final render and export. I checked every part as a valid solid, checked the nut pocket is open, and exported the STEP files. This is the finished back view.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/6390ba466bf6a0de7c916a73c9beb745ecb11124c67e0acdc1bf68c674744cb5.png)

Total Hours Worked = 13 Hours

### 2026-10-10 – Hour 1: Setting the lean and the floor

**10h**

Hour 1: Setting the lean and the floor

The camera’s USB-C port is on its bottom edge, so the dock has to stand the camera upright with the port pointing down onto an Apple USB-C plug. I started with a floor plane and tilted the camera model back 12°, so the screen is readable and the camera leans against the rear wall. The floor sits at the bottom of the camera’s four corner bumpers, so the camera’s weight rests on the bumpers and never on the connector.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/5b94fb5e9c29a97a4650c43e5b0d3b4de672f783fc90db65d43a729d46b526cc.png)

Hour 2: Wedge base

I modelled a rounded-corner base that is tall at the front, with a long ramp sloping down at the back. When the camera leans back, its center of mass ends up behind the cradle, and the ramp gives the dock enough footprint to keep it from tipping. I kept the camera ghosted above the base to check the proportions.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/b67f3f560eaef15967361ce0246a30037a4c79cc66814d7d4d81a01aee1d9dc9.png)

Hour 3: Walls

I added the rear wall, two side walls and two short front tabs. I built them in the camera’s own tilted frame so they stay square to the floor, then fused them onto the base. The front is open between the two tabs so the camera lifts out with a finger.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/0e3f02a1d9d2f01f17a8299af8cfb27b28186add2f6c2b260ae1839c1a5975f6.png)

Hour 4: Pocket and lanyard notch

I cut the pocket with 0.8 mm of clearance around the camera and its bumpers. I also cut a notch in the right wall so the lanyard eye clears the dock. Then I put the camera in to check that it seats and leans back as planned.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/1c5d29a0c30fe5c4ebe0325a0de5e4fdce0d603a25717e858bf572bbf0e59148.png)

Hour 5: Plug channel

I cut a tilted channel straight down from the camera’s USB-C opening, so the camera drops straight onto the plug. I added four small ribs on the channel walls to grip the plug body.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/8bddf09a50991b9db2da5071c74c07e62c59d807517be8c4b4e875e5056b24f1.png)

Hour 6: Underside

On the bottom I cut a recess for the base plate, a weight bay, six M3 insert holes and a cable exit through the rear edge. I also added grip lines on the sides and a recess on the front for the name plate.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/1e9d06b2c669caabccf5288eced04197a0bd2572ffe31a067f56071cd276ac10.png)

Hour 7: Base plate

The plate screws on from below and carries the cable. It has a groove that routes the cable to the rear and two small posts that hold the plug up from below. It also has six screw holes and four rubber-foot pockets.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/cd1f90b4312ae5fcf464edc57b0b550b355c2e37fa3498a842b595db2960af9c.png)

Hour 8: Checking the fit

I added a reference Apple USB-C plug and cable and cut a section through the plug to see how everything sits. The cable runs down the channel and out through the groove at the back. An overlap check on the dock, camera case, plug and cable found no collisions. The ribs overlap the plug by about 5 mm³, which is the intended grip.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/dd5945eb9fc2f53500f19e433ea0caf1586afa19d39376c2fe02b21891b4f393.png)

Hour 9-10: Name plate and final dock

I put “Pocket Thermal” on the front in cursive, as raised orange letters on a dark recessed plate. Then I exported the STEP files, one with the dock alone and one with the dock, camera enclosure and cable.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/b6e2463b8bd4b0b192e0538ad09e6dc30594847983607e993d95135b2430e039.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/3CZrnXeGMnVu8EBY8O03M7MrPW0qoSbZ/4a031f7a9050f6dc382d482991274c54b23fd50b433a6fb80a9aab004ad544bb.png)

Final Hours this session: 10
